rows.explanation: The instability value of 0.83 is correct as a measurement, but it doesn't point to a design problem here. BorrowBookUseCase is an application-layer orchestrator. Its outgoing dependencies (lines 1-10) all point inward to stable abstractions: domain entities, errors, repository interfaces, a domain service, a value object, and the application's own DTO and ports (Clock and IdGenerator, lines 9-10). Nothing imports infrastructure. Its collaborators come in through the constructor (lines 22-28), so they can be swapped at the composition root. Few modules depend on it, which is normal for a use case: it is the entry point a driver calls, not something other code builds on. The Stable Dependencies Principle expects concrete use cases like this to be highly unstable, because they depend on stable things and almost nothing depends on them. The real problem would be the reverse: domain or shared modules depending on this class. The body (lines 30-43) only coordinates domain behaviour (policy check, book.checkOut, Loan.open, saves). It doesn't absorb logic that would make it a widely depended-on hub. The high score comes from the measure itself, not from a flaw in this design.
rows.fix: No code change is needed. Change FF-C03's configuration so it doesn't apply a low instability threshold to concrete application use cases. Either exempt src/application/use-cases/** or allow a high ceiling (for example ≤ 1.0) for leaf orchestrators. Keep strict thresholds for domain and application ports/DTOs, and pair the rule with a check that dependencies point toward more stable modules.

Lines 4-10 hold a code-to-status table: three NOT_FOUND codes map to 404 and two validation codes map to 400. Line 13 branches on `instanceof DomainError`, looks up the status, and falls back to 409 when a code has no entry. Line 14 maps every other error to a generic 500. Cover four cases: a DomainError with a mapped NOT_FOUND code returns 404; a DomainError with INVALID_ISBN or INVALID_BOOK returns 400; a DomainError with an unmapped code returns 409 and keeps its message; and a plain Error or non-Error value returns 500 with 'Internal error'.

rows.explanation: FF-CV03 is meant to catch two things: classes that use a Repository-style name but aren't repositories, and repositories that aren't named as repositories. `CsvReportWriter` in src/infrastructure/http/CsvReportWriter.ts is neither. Its name contains no repository term (line 4). Its only method, `write`, is a pure transformation (lines 5-8): it maps an in-memory `readonly LoanDto[]` into CSV rows (line 6) and returns the joined string with a header (line 7). It doesn't store, load, query or delete anything, and it doesn't touch a database, file system or collection, so it doesn't act as a repository that should carry the suffix. The only import is an application DTO (line 1), and there's no persistence dependency. I ignored the doc comment on line 3 when judging; the decision comes from what the method body does. The class is a formatter, and calling it a "Writer" is accurate. The rule most likely matched on a broad pattern such as the word "Write" or "Writer", or a method named `write`, and treated it as a sign of persistence. That makes this a false positive of the rule's mechanism, not a naming violation.
rows.fix: No code change is needed. The rule should stop treating "Writer" class names or `write` methods as signs of a repository. It should only flag a class as an unnamed repository when it has real persistence behaviour, such as depending on a database, ORM, file system or storage client, or having CRUD-style methods (save/find/delete) on an entity. Pure functions that turn data into a string, like this one, should be excluded.

rows.explanation: src/infrastructure/http/ErrorMapper.ts has behaviour worth testing, so the missing paired test file is a real gap and not a trivial-file artefact. Lines 4-10 hold a code-to-status table: three NOT_FOUND codes map to 404 and two validation codes map to 400. Line 13 branches on `instanceof DomainError`, looks up the status, and falls back to 409 when a code has no entry. Line 14 maps every other error to a generic 500. Each of these paths could regress without anyone noticing. For example, a renamed domain error code would quietly drop from 404 to 409, and a change to the `instanceof` check could leak a 500 where a domain error was expected. This mapping sets the HTTP contract clients see, and it can be tested in isolation because it is a pure function with no I/O. A paired test is cheap here and clearly what the rule is meant to require.
rows.fix: Add src/infrastructure/http/ErrorMapper.test.ts (or the project's usual test location) to test `toErrorResponse`. Cover four cases: a DomainError with a mapped NOT_FOUND code returns 404; a DomainError with INVALID_ISBN or INVALID_BOOK returns 400; a DomainError with an unmapped code returns 409 and keeps its message; and a plain Error or non-Error value returns 500 with 'Internal error'.

Its outgoing dependencies are what you would expect from an adapter: three application use cases (src/infrastructure/http/LoanController.ts lines 1-3) and two HTTP helpers in the same folder (lines 4-5). It gets these through constructor injection (lines 8-12). Each method does the same thin job: turn the request into use-case input, call the use case, and map the result or error to an HTTP response (lines 14-36). It contains no business logic. In a layered or clean architecture the outermost layer is supposed to be unstable, so a high instability value is expected here. Very little should depend on a controller, apart from the composition root or router. An instability of 0.83 for this file is normal for its position in the design, not a sign of fragility. The real stability concerns are domain and application code becoming unstable or depending outward, and this file does neither: every dependency points inward or to sibling infrastructure helpers.
rows.fix: Set FF-C03's instability threshold per layer. Either exempt the infrastructure layer (kind: infrastructure) or allow it values near 1.0, and keep strict, low thresholds for domain and application, where stability actually matters.

rows.label: unscored
rows.explanation: src/infrastructure/http/ErrorMapper.ts has behaviour worth testing, so the missing paired test file is a real gap and not a trivial-file artefact. Lines 4-10 hold a code-to-status table: three NOT_FOUND codes map to 404 and two validation codes map to 400. Line 13 branches on `instanceof DomainError`, looks up the status, and falls back to 409 when a code has no entry. Line 14 maps every other error to a generic 500. Each of these paths could regress without anyone noticing. For example, a renamed domain error code would quietly drop from 404 to 409, and a change to the `instanceof` check could leak a 500 where a domain error was expected. This mapping sets the HTTP contract clients see, and it can be tested in isolation because it is a pure function with no I/O. A paired test is cheap here and clearly what the rule is meant to require.
rows.fix: Add src/infrastructure/http/ErrorMapper.test.ts (or the project's usual test location) to test `toErrorResponse`. Cover four cases: a DomainError with a mapped NOT_FOUND code returns 404; a DomainError with INVALID_ISBN or INVALID_BOOK returns 400; a DomainError with an unmapped code returns 409 and keeps its message; and a plain Error or non-Error value returns 500 with 'Internal error'.

rows.label: unscored
rows.explanation: The rule correctly reports that src/infrastructure/persistence/InMemoryMemberRepository.ts has no paired test file, but this file does not carry the risk the rule targets. The class is an in-memory implementation of the domain's MemberRepository port (lines 1-4). It holds only a private Map (line 5). findById passes straight through to Map.get (lines 7-9), and save passes straight through to Map.set keyed by member.id (lines 11-13). There is no branching, no validation, no mapping or serialization, and no error handling. A dedicated unit test would only check the behaviour of the built-in Map. Adapters like this are normally fakes used to run application-layer use cases, so they get exercised by those tests anyway. The missing test file is a side effect of applying "one test per source file" mechanically, not a real gap in test coverage of project logic.
rows.fix: Change FF-CV05's configuration so trivial in-memory adapters are not required to have a paired test. For example, exclude src/infrastructure/persistence/InMemory*.ts, or skip files with no branching logic. If the project wants coverage of the repository contract, add one shared MemberRepository contract test suite that runs against every implementation, rather than a separate test file for each fake.

Its outgoing dependencies (lines 1-10) all point inward to stable abstractions: domain entities, errors, repository interfaces, a domain service, a value object, and the application's own DTO and ports (Clock and IdGenerator, lines 9-10). Nothing imports infrastructure. Its collaborators come in through the constructor (lines 22-28), so they can be swapped at the composition root. Few modules depend on it, which is normal for a use case: it is the entry point a driver calls, not something other code builds on. The Stable Dependencies Principle expects concrete use cases like this to be highly unstable, because they depend on stable things and almost nothing depends on them. The real problem would be the reverse: domain or shared modules depending on this class. The body (lines 30-43) only coordinates domain behaviour (policy check, book.checkOut, Loan.open, saves). It doesn't absorb logic that would make it a widely depended-on hub. The high score comes from the measure itself, not from a flaw in this design.
rows.fix: No code change is needed. Change FF-C03's configuration so it doesn't apply a low instability threshold to concrete application use cases. Either exempt src/application/use-cases/** or allow a high ceiling (for example ≤ 1.0) for leaf orchestrators. Keep strict thresholds for domain and application ports/DTOs, and pair the rule with a check that dependencies point toward more stable modules.

rows.explanation: This is a real layer violation. The domain service at src/domain/services/LoanPolicy.ts imports the concrete infrastructure class SystemClock on line 4 and creates it directly on line 7 (`new SystemClock()`). Line 10 then uses it to read the wall clock. So the domain layer depends on the outermost layer, which is the opposite of the inward dependency direction the layer model requires. The import also creates a transitive cycle. SystemClock (src/infrastructure/system/SystemClock.ts lines 1-3) implements the application port Clock, so domain → infrastructure → application, even though application normally depends on domain. The hidden clock also makes isOverdueToday non-deterministic and hard to test. The rest of the class already shows the right pattern: assertCanBorrow (line 13) takes `now: Date` as a parameter instead of reading a clock.
rows.fix: In LoanPolicy.ts, delete the SystemClock import (line 4) and the field (line 7). Change isOverdueToday to take the current time as an argument, for example `isOverdueAt(loan: Loan, now: Date): boolean { return loan.isOverdue(now); }`, the same way assertCanBorrow already does. The application use case that calls it should get `now` from the injected Clock port (application/ports/Clock), and the composition root should wire SystemClock to that port.

rows.explanation: This is a real violation. src/domain/entities/Member.ts sits in the domain layer, and line 1 imports `Request` from the transport framework express. The import is type-only, so nothing from express loads at runtime. It still matters, because the type is actually used: the static factory `fromRequest` on lines 15-18 takes an express `Request`, reads `request.body` and maps its untyped fields into the constructor. That puts HTTP request parsing inside a domain entity and ties the domain's compile-time API to express. The domain can't be built or reused without express's types, and a change in the transport layer would force a change in the entity. The real domain logic, the invariant checks on lines 11-12, needs nothing from express. This is exactly the coupling FF-P01 exists to prevent.
rows.fix: Delete the `import type { Request } from 'express'` on line 1 and the `fromRequest` method on lines 15-18 from Member.ts. Put the mapping from request to entity in an infrastructure HTTP adapter or controller, for example under src/infrastructure/http. That adapter should read `req.body` and call `new Member(id, name, email, maxActiveLoans)`, or pass a plain DTO to an application use case that builds the Member.

rows.explanation: src/business/ServiceFactory.ts is a composition root. A module like this always has high fan-out and fan-in of about one (its startup caller), so instability ≈ 6/7 = 0.857 comes from what the module is, not from a design flaw. The rule exists to stop stable code from depending on volatile code, and that doesn't apply here. The factory has no domain logic, its only consumer is startup code that is meant to be unstable, and its dependencies point downward from business to persistence, which closed layering allows (the comment on lines 13-16 says this is intended). Business services are exposed through the BusinessServices interface (lines 8-11), and the factory doesn't make them any less stable. rows.label: unscored
rows.explanation: The rule is about naming: Repository names should go only on repositories, and repositories should be called that. `SalesReportService` doesn't break either half. It has no Repository suffix, so the name isn't being misused. It also isn't a repository under another name. It doesn't load, save or provide collection-style access to aggregates. It runs one reporting calculation: it goes through the `orders` table, keeps only placed orders, adds up line totals minus discounts and returns a domain `Money` value (src/business/services/SalesReportService.ts:9-16). It sits in `src/business/services` and is declared as a service (line 6), which matches what it does. The rule most likely fired because the class takes `InMemoryDatabase` directly and reads `OrderRecord` rows (lines 1-2, 7, 11). That is a real design smell: a business class depends on the persistence layer, which the comment on line 5 admits. But that's a layering and dependency problem, not a naming problem. Renaming the class `SalesReportRepository` would hide the domain calculation it does and wouldn't fix the dependency.
rows.fix: Change FF-CV03 so it doesn't treat "depends on the database" as meaning "is an unnamed repository". It should only flag a class as a repository with the wrong name if it actually exposes repository behaviour, such as find/get/save/delete methods that return or store entities or records. A class that only computes aggregates should not count. Leave the business→persistence dependency in this class (lines 1-2, 7) to the layering rule. The real fix there is a read-model or gateway interface in persistence that `SalesReportService` uses.

Lines 3-9 do only declare the `OrderViewModel` interface, but `renderOrder` (lines 11-19) is an exported function with real logic. It maps a domain `Order` into a presentation model. The rule is advisory, so this is a low-severity finding, but it is real.
rows.fix: Add src/presentation/views/OrderView.test.ts, using the project's existing test naming convention. It should build an `Order` fixture with at least two lines and a non-zero discount, call `renderOrder`, and check four things: `id` and `status` are copied over; each entry in `lines` has the right sku and quantity and a formatted total; `discount` equals `order.discount.format()`; and `total` equals `order.total().format()`. Also add a case with an empty `lines` array.

rows.label: true
rows.explanation: This project uses Fowler's classic layering, and the persistence code is built that way: `ProductGateway` is a Table Data Gateway (src/persistence/ProductGateway.ts:5) that hands plain persistence records (`ProductRecord`) back to whoever calls it (lines 9-11 and 18-20). In that design the domain logic calls the gateways, so business sits above persistence and persistence must not depend on business. Line 1 imports the business value object `Money`, and `priceOf` (lines 13-16) builds a domain object with `Money.ofCents(row.priceCents)`. That is a real upward dependency, not a quirk of the rule. It also pulls business validation into the data-source layer: `Money.ofCents` can throw `BusinessError` (src/business/model/Money.ts:7-9). And since business code almost certainly uses this gateway, the two layers would depend on each other in a cycle. The rest of the gateway only needs its own layer (`./Database`, `./records/ProductRecord`). So the one method that turns a stored row into a domain type is exactly the leak the rule is meant to catch.
rows.fix: Delete `priceOf` and the `Money` import from src/persistence/ProductGateway.ts. If a raw price lookup is still useful, have the gateway return `row.priceCents` as a number. Then do the `Money.ofCents(record.priceCents)` conversion in the business layer (for example in the service or domain code that calls `findBySku`), so persistence only works with records and plain values.

rows.label: true
rows.explanation: The project follows classic layering: presentation → business → persistence. src/persistence/ProductGateway.ts lines 5-6 describe the class as a Fowler Table Data Gateway, a data-source component that the domain layer calls. In that style the persistence layer must not depend on the business layer. Yet line 1 imports Money from src/business/model/Money.ts, and lines 13-16 (`priceOf`) build a domain value object with `Money.ofCents(row.priceCents)`. That also pulls in business validation and errors (Money.ts lines 1 and 7-9). So persistence now depends on business, and business presumably uses the gateway, which creates a cycle between the two layers. The "skip" label is a bit off, because persistence and business are next to each other and this is really an upward dependency. Even so, the import is one the strict layer model does not allow, which is what FF-S03 exists to catch. The rest of the gateway (lines 9-29) deals only in ProductRecord rows, so `priceOf` is the only thing breaking the layering.
rows.fix: Remove `priceOf` and the Money import from ProductGateway (lines 1 and 13-16). Have business-layer callers call `gateway.findBySku(sku)` and wrap the raw `priceCents` themselves with `Money.ofCents(...)`. If a price lookup is needed, the gateway can expose `priceCentsOf(sku): number | undefined` instead. Separately, the rule's message should label this case as an upward or reverse dependency, not LAYER_SKIP.

Line 9 creates the repository directly (`new InMemoryRegistrationRepository()`), and line 12 calls it to read persisted data. So the domain service depends on a specific storage implementation and on NestJS. The repository already implements a domain-owned port, RegistrationRepository (in-memory-registration.repository.ts lines 3, 6). That means the right inward-pointing abstraction exists, and the domain is skipping it. There is a second problem: because the policy creates its own private store, it reads from a different in-memory map than the one the app's DI container shares, so `registrationsOf` would probably return nothing. Meanwhile, `assertCanRegister` (lines 15-22) already takes `existing` registrations as a parameter, so the policy doesn't need to fetch data itself.

This file holds real domain behaviour that a test should pin down, so it is not trivial code like a type-only module, a barrel or plain config. rows.explanation: The fan-out of 12 is accurate, but it comes from a single, cohesive use-case orchestrator in a hexagonal application layer, not from a module with tangled responsibilities. Every import is either a domain type or service (src/application/services/BookRoomService.ts lines 1-5) or a port the application layer owns (lines 6-12). There are no imports from adapters, infrastructure or frameworks. The five outbound dependencies are injected as port interfaces through the constructor (lines 18-24). The class has one public method, `book` (lines 26-43), which runs one business transaction in a straight line: load room and guest, validate, check availability, price, charge, save, notify, map to a view. Each import is used exactly once for that flow, and several are just command/view DTO types (lines 6-7). Coordinating ports and domain services like this is what an application service is for in this layer model. Splitting it would scatter one use case across several classes without removing any real coupling. So this is a threshold artefact on sound code, not a module that knows too much.
rows.fix: Leave the code as it is. In the FF-C02 configuration, either raise the fan-out threshold for application-layer services (src/application/services/**), or count only concrete or cross-layer dependencies. That would mean not counting imports of the application's own port interfaces (src/application/ports/**) and pure domain types, so that use-case orchestrators wired through ports don't trip the rule.

rows.explanation: src/config/container.ts is the project's composition root. The comment at line 19 says so, and the code matches: it builds every concrete adapter (lines 21-25), passes them into the application services (lines 27, 29-30) and hands those services to the inbound controllers and CLI (lines 28-32). Its 11 imports (lines 1-11) are the reason a composition root exists. It has to know each concrete outbound adapter, application service and inbound adapter so that no other module needs to. The fan-out rule is meant to catch modules that take on too many responsibilities or couple to too much. This file has none of that: it holds no business logic, does nothing beyond construction, and every import is used only to wire one object into another. Splitting it up or cutting its imports would spread the wiring knowledge to other places, which is worse architecture. A fan-out of 11 is just the threshold being hit by correct composition-root code.
rows.fix: Exempt composition-root modules (for example src/config/container.ts, or the whole config layer) from FF-C02, or give them a higher fan-out threshold. Wiring modules are expected to import every concrete adapter and service.

rows.explanation: The instability measurement of 0.92 is accurate, but it doesn't point to a design problem. BookRoomService is the concrete implementation of an inbound use-case port (`implements BookRoom`, line 14). In a hexagonal layout, a class like this is a leaf: callers reach it only through the `BookRoom` port, and the composition root wires it up. Its afferent coupling should therefore be close to zero. Its outgoing dependencies (lines 1-12) all point to stable code: domain errors, models and services (lines 1-5), and port interfaces in `../ports/in` and `../ports/out` (lines 6-12). Nothing points to adapters or config. The outbound collaborators come in through the constructor as port abstractions (lines 18-24), and the method body (lines 26-43) only orchestrates calls to them. That matches the Stable Dependencies Principle: an unstable, easy-to-change class depends on stable abstractions, and no other code depends on it. High instability is the expected and correct value for a concrete use-case implementation. This is a threshold artefact on sound code, not a fragile component that others rely on.

Another is to compute instability per component or package, not per file. Either way, concrete use-case implementations under src/application/services/** should be exempt, because near-maximal instability is intended for them.

Lines 10-15 validate the checkIn/checkOut query parameters with DateRange.parse. They turn a BookingError into an HTTP 400 response and rethrow every other error. Lines 16-20 coerce the query values with String() and Number(), and default guests to 1 when it is absent (line 19). Line 21 maps a successful result to a 200 response. Each of these is a branch that can break unnoticed: the error mapping, the rethrow path, the guests default, and the coercion of missing parameters to the string 'undefined'. The FindAvailableRooms port is injected through the constructor (line 7), so the controller is easy to unit-test with a stub. Nothing in the layer model exempts presentation adapters from having tests.
rows.fix: Add src/adapters/inbound/http/RoomController.test.ts (or put it in the project's test folder) using a stub FindAvailableRooms. It should check that: (1) invalid or reversed dates return status 400 with the BookingError message; (2) a non-BookingError thrown by DateRange.parse is rethrown; (3) valid input calls find with checkIn, checkOut and guests defaulting to 1, and returns status 200 with the rooms; (4) an explicit guests query value is passed through as a number.

Coordinating ports and domain services like this is what an application service is for in this layer model. Splitting it would scatter one use case across several classes without removing any real coupling. So this is a threshold artefact on sound code, not a module that knows too much.
rows.fix: Leave the code as it is. In the FF-C02 configuration, either raise the fan-out threshold for application-layer services (src/application/services/**), or count only concrete or cross-layer dependencies. That would mean not counting imports of the application's own port interfaces (src/application/ports/**) and pure domain types, so that use-case orchestrators wired through ports don't trip the rule.

rows.label: unscored
rows.explanation: src/config/container.ts is the project's composition root. The comment at line 19 says so, and the code matches: it builds every concrete adapter (lines 21-25), passes them into the application services (lines 27, 29-30) and hands those services to the inbound controllers and CLI (lines 28-32). Its 11 imports (lines 1-11) are the reason a composition root exists. It has to know each concrete outbound adapter, application service and inbound adapter so that no other module needs to. The fan-out rule is meant to catch modules that take on too many responsibilities or couple to too much. This file has none of that: it holds no business logic, does nothing beyond construction, and every import is used only to wire one object into another. Splitting it up or cutting its imports would spread the wiring knowledge to other places, which is worse architecture. A fan-out of 11 is just the threshold being hit by correct composition-root code.
rows.fix: Exempt composition-root modules (for example src/config/container.ts, or the whole config layer) from FF-C02, or give them a higher fan-out threshold. Wiring modules are expected to import every concrete adapter and service.

rows.label: unscored
rows.explanation: The instability measurement of 0.92 is accurate, but it doesn't point to a design problem. BookRoomService is the concrete implementation of an inbound use-case port (`implements BookRoom`, line 14). In a hexagonal layout, a class like this is a leaf: callers reach it only through the `BookRoom` port, and the composition root wires it up. Its afferent coupling should therefore be close to zero. Its outgoing dependencies (lines 1-12) all point to stable code: domain errors, models and services (lines 1-5), and port interfaces in `../ports/in` and `../ports/out` (lines 6-12). Nothing points to adapters or config. The outbound collaborators come in through the constructor as port abstractions (lines 18-24), and the method body (lines 26-43) only orchestrates calls to them. That matches the Stable Dependencies Principle: an unstable, easy-to-change class depends on stable abstractions, and no other code depends on it. High instability is the expected and correct value for a concrete use-case implementation. This is a threshold artefact on sound code, not a fragile component that others rely on.
rows.fix: No code change is needed. One option is to change FF-C03 so the instability threshold for the application layer applies only to port modules (src/application/ports/**). Another is to compute instability per component or package, not per file. Either way, concrete use-case implementations under src/application/services/** should be exempt, because near-maximal instability is intended for them.

rows.label: unscored
rows.explanation: The instability of 0.875 is accurate as a number, but here it reflects sound hexagonal design rather than a problem. CancelBookingService is a concrete use-case implementation. It implements the inbound port CancelBooking (src/application/services/CancelBookingService.ts:9) and depends only on abstractions: the domain error (line 1), inbound port types (lines 2-3) and four outbound port interfaces passed in through the constructor (lines 4-7, 10-15). Nothing else should depend on it directly. Callers should use the CancelBooking port, and only the composition root in config should create the service. That gives it many outgoing dependencies and about one incoming one (7/(7+1) = 0.875), which is what you expect from a leaf implementation. By the Stable Dependencies / Stable Abstractions principles, the port interfaces should be stable and their implementations unstable, and that is the case here. The method body (lines 17-26) only coordinates calls through ports and domain behaviour (booking.cancel() on line 20). It does not reach into adapters or infrastructure. There is no layering leak or fragile hub, so a stricter threshold would be measuring a correct design.
rows.fix: No code change needed. Change FF-C03 so concrete service implementations in the application layer (for example src/application/services/**) are exempt from the instability threshold, or get a high one (≥0.9). Keep the low-instability threshold only for abstractions such as src/application/ports/** and src/domain/**. Another option is to combine instability with abstractness, i.e. use distance from the main sequence instead of raw instability.

rows.label: unscored
rows.explanation: I'm dismissing this finding. FindAvailableRoomsService is a concrete use-case implementation, and in a hexagonal layout this kind of class should be unstable. Its outgoing dependencies all point toward more abstract or more stable modules: the domain model and domain service (src/application/services/FindAvailableRoomsService.ts lines 1-2), the inbound port it implements (line 3, line 7), and the outbound port interfaces it receives through the constructor (lines 4-5, lines 10-13). Callers are supposed to depend on the FindAvailableRooms port rather than on this class, so in practice only the composition root in src/config should reference it. That explains the low afferent coupling and the instability of 0.83. The Stable Dependencies Principle is still satisfied, because the service depends on things more stable than itself, and nothing stable depends on it. The class is small and does one job (lines 15-21): it filters rooms using domain logic. So the high ratio comes from applying one threshold to the whole application layer, not from a design problem.
rows.fix: Change the FF-C03 configuration so concrete application services (src/application/services/**) are either exempt or get a high instability threshold (e.g. up to 1.0). Keep the strict, low threshold for the abstract port modules (src/application/ports/**) and for the domain, since those are the parts that need to stay stable.

rows.label: unscored
rows.explanation: src/config/container.ts is the project's composition root, and the comment on line 19 says so. Its job is to import concrete adapters and services (lines 1-11) and wire them together (lines 20-33). A composition root depends outward on everything, and only the entry point depends on it. So instability = Ce/(Ce+Ca) = 1 is what this kind of module should measure. It does not mean the module is fragile. Instability thresholds exist so that components many others depend on stay stable. Nothing in the domain, application or adapter layers depends on container.ts, so its high instability cannot spread change to them. The finding comes from a layer-model artefact: config is classified as kind "application", which gives it an application-layer stability threshold that does not suit a wiring module. The code itself is sound and uses the standard hexagonal composition-root pattern.
rows.fix: Give the config layer its own kind in the layer model (for example "composition-root"), or exclude src/config/** from FF-C03. A composition root's instability is expected to be at or near 1.

rows.label: unscored
rows.explanation: This file is mostly type definitions with nothing to run, so it has nothing worth testing on its own. Lines 1-10 declare two interfaces, `HttpRequest` and `HttpResponse`, which disappear when the code is compiled. The only runtime code is `HttpError` (lines 12-16), a trivial subclass of `Error`. Its constructor only stores `status` as a readonly field and passes `message` to `super`. There is no branching, validation or transformation, so a dedicated `HttpTypes.test.ts` could only check the language's own behaviour. These types and the error class are used and covered by the HTTP adapter's handler and controller tests. The rule wants each source file paired with a test file so that untested logic doesn't slip through. This file contains no such logic, so the missing test file is a gap in the rule's mechanism, not a real coverage problem.
rows.fix: Have FF-CV05 skip files that contain only type declarations or trivial `Error` subclasses with no logic. For example, skip files whose runtime statements are limited to classes whose constructors only call `super` and assign parameter properties. Another option is to let the project exclude shared type modules such as `**/*Types.ts` in the rule configuration.

rows.label: true
rows.explanation: Quantity is a domain value object (src/ordering/domain/value-objects/Quantity.ts, lines 1-2), but it is not immutable. It keeps its state in a field that is not readonly (`private current: number`, line 4), and it has a public `set value` accessor (lines 15-17) that writes to that field after construction. This setter also skips the positive-integer check the constructor runs on line 7, so any caller can set a constructed Quantity to 0, a negative number or a fraction. Because objects are shared by reference, changing one Quantity also changes it for every aggregate or collection holding the same instance. That is exactly the aliasing and invariant problem the value-object immutability rule exists to catch. The `plus` method (lines 19-21) already returns a new instance, which shows the class was meant to be immutable. The finding is a real violation and not a quirk of how the rule detects setters.
rows.fix: Delete the `set value` accessor (lines 15-17) and make the field readonly. For example, change line 4 to `private readonly current: number;` or use `readonly value: number` set in the constructor. Any code that called the setter should create a new Quantity instead (e.g. `new Quantity(v)` or a `withValue(v): Quantity` factory), so the constructor's validation always runs.

rows.label: true
rows.explanation: src/billing/api/InvoiceController.ts line 4 imports `GetOrderSummary` directly from `../../ordering/application/GetOrderSummary.js`. That path is inside the ordering context, so the billing controller's constructor (lines 6-7) depends on ordering's internals. `GetOrderSummary` (src/ordering/application/GetOrderSummary.ts lines 1-7) is ordering's concrete application service. It is wired to ordering's domain `OrderRepository` and `OrderId`, and its doc comment on line 5 says it implements the published `OrderSummaryQuery` contract. Billing only needs that contract, not this concrete class. The rule measured that this path is not part of ordering's public API. Even if ordering's barrel re-exports the class, reaching into the folder directly skips both the barrel and any anti-corruption layer. As a result, refactoring ordering's application layer can break billing, which is exactly the coupling between contexts that FF-DS02 exists to stop. The import is type-only, but billing still depends on ordering's internals at compile time.
rows.fix: Change line 4 to import the published contract through ordering's public API, for example `import type { OrderSummaryQuery } from '../../ordering/index.js'` (or ordering's contracts entry that the barrel exposes). Then type the constructor parameter on line 7 as `orders?: OrderSummaryQuery`, and have the composition root (src/main.ts) inject the concrete `GetOrderSummary`. Alternatively, put a billing-side ACL port in front of it.

rows.label: true
rows.explanation: This is a real aggregate-boundary violation. src/ordering/domain/order/OrderLine.ts lines 4-6 define OrderLine as an inner entity of the Order aggregate, meant to be reached only through Order. At line 4, src/ordering/application/GetOrderSummary.ts imports OrderLine directly. It is not an unused type import: the public method describeLine at lines 18-20 takes an OrderLine as a parameter and reads its lineNo, productId and subtotal(). That puts the inner entity into the application service's public API, so callers outside the aggregate have to hold and pass OrderLine instances. That is the coupling the rule exists to prevent. The rest of the class shows the correct pattern: summaryOf (lines 10-15) loads the aggregate through its root and asks only the root for data (order.total(), order.lineCount()). describeLine breaks that pattern. I based this on the code itself, not on the "VIOLATION" comment at line 17, which is project text.
rows.fix: Remove the OrderLine import at line 4 and change describeLine so it no longer takes an OrderLine. One option is to add a method on the Order root (for example order.lineDescriptions() or order.describeLine(lineNo)) that returns plain data, and call it through the repository-loaded aggregate. Another is to have the root return a read-only line DTO or value object (lineNo, productId, subtotalCents) and have describeLine format that instead of the entity.

rows.label: true
rows.explanation: This is a real violation. src/ordering/domain/order/OrderLine.ts line 4 says OrderLine is an inner entity of the Order aggregate that is "reachable only through Order", and its constructor and methods (lines 5-18) carry no aggregate-root identity of their own. Even so, src/ordering/domain/order/OrderLineRepository.ts lines 4-7 declare a repository for OrderLine. It has `byProduct` (line 5), which loads lines on their own outside any Order, and `save(line: OrderLine)` (line 6), which saves a single line apart from its root. Code using these methods can read or change order lines without going through Order. Order is the consistency boundary, so that skips Order's invariants (for example totals, or the merging of quantities in `increase`, lines 12-14). This is exactly what "repositories only for aggregate roots" is meant to stop. The finding is not caused by how the rule detects imports: the import on line 1 is there because the interface really is typed on the inner entity.
rows.fix: Delete OrderLineRepository. Load and save order lines only through the Order aggregate's repository: OrderRepository.save(order) saves the whole aggregate, lines included. Change line edits so they go through Order methods. If you need to look up "orders containing product X", add a query method to OrderRepository that returns Orders (for example `findByProduct(productId): Promise<Order[]>`), or use a separate read-model/query service in the application layer that returns DTOs instead of OrderLine entities.

rows.label: true
rows.explanation: Quantity is documented as a value object (src/ordering/domain/value-objects/Quantity.ts line 1) and sits in the domain layer. It is not immutable. The constructor parameter property `public value: number` on line 4 is a public field without `readonly`, so any caller can reassign it. `setValue` on lines 12-14 is a public mutator that overwrites `this.value`, and it skips the positive-integer check from line 5. That means a Quantity can end up holding 0, a negative number or a fraction even though its own rule forbids this. `plus` on lines 8-10 shows the intended style: it returns a new instance instead of changing the existing one. Both mutation routes the rule reports are real. Because Quantity can be changed in place, it can't be shared safely or compared by value, which is exactly what this rule is meant to prevent.
rows.fix: Change the constructor to `constructor(public readonly value: number)`. Delete `setValue`, or replace it with `withValue(value: number): Quantity { return new Quantity(value); }`, which returns a new, validated instance. Update callers to use the returned value.

rows.label: true
rows.explanation: src/billing/domain/invoice/value-objects/InvoiceId.ts sits under src/*/domain/**, so it belongs to the domain layer. Line 1 imports `plainToInstance` from `class-transformer`, which is a serialisation framework library, and line 10 actually calls it inside the value object's `fromPlain` factory (lines 9-11). That is not a stray type-only or unused import. The domain value object depends at runtime on a framework, which is exactly what a framework-free domain rule exists to prevent. Turning plain objects into instances is a persistence/transport concern, and it belongs in infrastructure or at the API edge. There is also a practical problem: class-transformer builds the instance with its own mechanism instead of the constructor's validated path. That can bypass or break the invariant check on line 6, so the coupling hurts correctness as well as purity. This is a real violation, not a false positive.
rows.fix: Remove the class-transformer import and the `plainToInstance` call from the domain. Write `fromPlain` as `static fromPlain(raw: { value: string }): InvoiceId { return new InvoiceId(raw.value); }` so construction always goes through the validating constructor. Any class-transformer-based mapping that is still needed should move to a mapper or DTO in src/billing/infrastructure/** or src/billing/api/**.

rows.label: true
rows.explanation: src/billing/application/InvoiceIssued.ts is in the application layer (src/*/application/**). It defines `InvoiceIssued`, which implements the shared-kernel `DomainEvent` contract (lines 1 and 4). The class has a domain-qualified event name, 'billing.invoice-issued' (line 5), and carries only domain data: an occurrence timestamp and the invoice and order identifiers (lines 6–8). It records a business fact of the billing aggregate. It is not an application-level integration message or command, and it does no orchestration or calls into infrastructure. Nothing in the class needs anything from the application layer. Because it sits under application/, the billing domain model can't raise or refer to it without depending upward on the application layer. That is exactly the problem FF-DT05 is meant to catch. The decision rests on the code itself, not on the comment at line 3.
rows.fix: Move the `InvoiceIssued` class to src/billing/domain/events/InvoiceIssued.ts (or src/billing/domain/InvoiceIssued.ts) and keep its `DomainEvent` import from the shared kernel. Have the Invoice aggregate in the domain raise it. Then update the imports in application, infrastructure and API code to point to the domain location.

rows.label: true
rows.explanation: This is a real violation. The finding counts methods, but the problem the rule targets is in what those private helpers do: they hold billing business rules. In src/billing/application/IssueInvoice.ts, `applyVolumeDiscount` (lines 21-23) gives a 5% discount on orders over 100,000 cents. `effectiveTaxRate` (lines 25-27) sets tax to zero for orders under 1,000 cents. `roundToCents` (lines 29-31) decides how money is rounded. `execute` (lines 11-19) applies all three before it calls the `Invoice` aggregate (lines 15-17). These are pricing and tax rules for the Invoice/Money domain. In the layer model they belong in src/*/domain/** (or the shared kernel for rounding), not in an application service. Keeping them here makes `Invoice` anemic about its own pricing invariants, and any other use case that issues invoices would have to copy them. A thin service would only load the order, call the aggregate or a domain service, and save. So the method count is a symptom of a real problem, not a threshold artefact.
rows.fix: Move the rules into the domain layer. Add a domain policy, for example `src/billing/domain/invoice/InvoicePricingPolicy.ts`, that owns the volume discount and the small-order tax exemption. Put the rounding in `Money` (for example `Money.ofRounded` or `Money.multiply` with a rounding mode). Then have `Invoice` apply the policy, for example `invoice.chargeOrder(order.orderId, amount, policy)` followed by `invoice.issue(policy.taxRateFor(amount))`. `IssueInvoice.execute` should only fetch the order, create the invoice, call domain methods and save. Remove the three private helpers.

rows.label: true
rows.explanation: In this layer model, each bounded context is a top-level directory under src/ with domain/application/infrastructure/acl/api subfolders. Shared code has one sanctioned home, src/shared-kernel/**, and src/main.ts is the composition root. src/utils/formatCurrency.ts fits none of these. `utils` is not a declared context and has none of the layer subfolders, so the file is reported in layer "none". The file exports a free-floating helper, `formatCurrency` (src/utils/formatCurrency.ts lines 2-4), that any context can import. That is the kind of ownerless "utils" module this rule is meant to stop: it sidesteps context boundaries and the shared-kernel agreement. The comment on line 1 is project data and played no part in this decision. The conclusion comes from where the file sits compared with the declared globs.
rows.fix: Give the helper an owner. If several contexts really share currency formatting, move it to src/shared-kernel/ (for example, src/shared-kernel/money/formatCurrency.ts, ideally as part of a Money value object). If only one context uses it for display, move it into that context's presentation layer (for example, src/<context>/api/formatCurrency.ts). Then delete src/utils/.

rows.label: true
rows.explanation: The rule caught a real violation. In src/billing/application/IssueInvoice.ts, line 7 imports the `Order` aggregate root directly from ordering's internal domain model (src/ordering/domain/order/Order.ts), not through ordering's public API or an anti-corruption layer. The import is used at lines 22-24, where `executeFor` takes an `Order` and reads `order.id.value`. That ties billing to ordering's internal structure, including the `OrderId` value object on line 15 of Order.ts. The class already has a proper boundary: the `OrderSource` port (line 5, used at lines 11 and 14-17) returns a billing-side view of an order (`orderId`, `currency`, `amountCents`). So the direct domain import adds cross-context coupling for no real benefit. Being type-only does not make it acceptable, because billing still depends on the shape of ordering's model and breaks when that model changes. The comment on line 6 is not taken as evidence; the import and its use alone show the problem.
rows.fix: Delete the `Order` import on line 7 and the `executeFor(invoiceId, order: Order)` method on lines 22-24. Callers should call `execute(invoiceId, orderId)` with a plain order ID string and let the `OrderSource` port (backed by an ordering public API or ACL adapter in src/billing/acl or infrastructure) supply the billable data. If a typed order reference is needed, use a type exported from ordering's public API or a billing-owned DTO.

rows.label: true
rows.explanation: The Customer aggregate root in src/ordering/domain/customer/Customer.ts belongs to the domain layer. On line 3 it does a type-only import of PlaceOrderCommand from src/ordering/application/PlaceOrder.ts, which is in the application layer. Line 19 uses that type in the `owns(cmd: PlaceOrderCommand)` method. Being type-only does not make this harmless: the domain's public API is now tied to an application-layer use-case DTO. PlaceOrder.ts also imports from the domain (lines 2-7), including the customer folder (lines 5-6), so the two layers depend on each other in a cycle. This is exactly the inward/downward violation that FF-S01 is meant to catch, and the comment on line 2 openly labels it as one.
rows.fix: Remove the application import from Customer.ts. Change `owns` to take a domain value, for example `owns(customerId: CustomerId): boolean { return customerId.value === this.id.value; }`. Then have PlaceOrder (application) call `customer.owns(new CustomerId(cmd.customerId))`. Another option is to drop `owns` and keep the ownership check in the application service.

rows.label: true
rows.explanation: This is a real layering violation. The import is type-only, but the presentation adapter still depends on the concrete persistence class. In src/ordering/api/OrderController.ts, line 3 imports InMemoryOrderRepository from the infrastructure layer. Line 7 then uses it as the type of an optional constructor parameter `repo`. That ties the inbound HTTP adapter to one specific storage implementation and skips both the application layer and the domain port. InMemoryOrderRepository implements the domain port OrderRepository (src/ordering/infrastructure/InMemoryOrderRepository.ts lines 2 and 5), so a proper abstraction exists and should be used instead. The controller doesn't even need the repository: `post` only calls `this.placeOrder.execute` (lines 9-12), so `repo` is unused. The controller's correct dependency is the application use case imported on line 1. The layer model allows no api→infrastructure dependency, and wiring concrete adapters belongs in the composition root (src/main.ts). The flagged import is exactly the sideways reach this rule is meant to catch.
rows.fix: Delete the import on line 3 of src/ordering/api/OrderController.ts and remove the unused optional `repo` parameter from the constructor on line 7, so the controller depends only on the PlaceOrder use case. If the controller ever needs a repository, it should depend on an application-layer service or the domain `OrderRepository` port, and src/main.ts should inject the InMemoryOrderRepository.
